10031:
Classical Pentecostalism teaches that after conversion believers should seek the baptism in the Holy Spirit, a distinct experience in which the Spirit comes upon them in power, as at Pentecost, normally evidenced by speaking in tongues. Its primary purpose is empowerment for witness and service, but Pentecostals see it as transforming the whole life, deepening intimacy with God, love for Christ and boldness in holiness.

Pentecostals divide on sanctification itself. Wesleyan Pentecostals (Church of God in Christ, Church of God of Cleveland, the Pentecostal Holiness Church) hold three stages: conversion, entire sanctification, then Spirit baptism. 'Finished Work' Pentecostals (the Assemblies of God and most later bodies), following William Durham, hold that sanctification is grounded in Christ's finished work at conversion and progresses through life, with Spirit baptism as a further, empowering experience. Common to both is the conviction that holiness and power come by an experiential encounter with the Spirit, not by doctrine and effort alone.

Pentecostalism emerged from the Holiness movement, whose preachers had already used 'baptism with the Holy Ghost' for entire sanctification. Parham's identification of tongues as evidence (1901) and the Azusa Street revival (1906–1909) turned this into a distinct movement. Within a few years Durham's Finished Work teaching split Pentecostals over whether sanctification is a second crisis. The Assemblies of God formed at Hot Springs, Arkansas, in 1914 and adopted its Statement of Fundamental Truths in 1916, affirming Spirit baptism as distinct from and subsequent to the new birth.

Pentecostalism became one of the fastest-growing movements in Christian history, especially in the global South. In scholarship, James Dunn's *Baptism in the Holy Spirit* (1970) and Frederick Dale Bruner's *A Theology of the Holy Spirit* (1970) challenged subsequence; Pentecostal scholars such as Stronstad and Robert Menzies replied by distinguishing Luke's and Paul's emphases.

10097:
Eastern Orthodox theology understands salvation and holiness as theosis or deification: humans, created in God's image, are called to grow into his likeness by participating in the divine life. Following Athanasius' summary that the Word became human so that humans might become divine, Orthodox teach that believers become by grace what God is by nature, without ceasing to be creatures and without merging into God's essence. Gregory Palamas' distinction between God's unknowable essence and his uncreated energies explains how real union with God is possible without pantheism.

Theosis is a lifelong, indeed endless, process of synergy, the cooperation of human freedom with divine grace. It is nourished by baptism, chrismation and above all the eucharist, by repentance and confession, by prayer (especially the Jesus Prayer), fasting and ascetic struggle, and by the virtues, chiefly love and humility. Its fruit is the acquisition of the Holy Spirit, as Seraphim of Sarov put it, and a transfigured life that radiates God's light. There is no single crisis, but there are moments of illumination; the saints are the evidence that the process is real.
10098: Athanasius argued that the incarnation of the Word restores humanity's corrupted image and makes possible human participation in God; his summary that God became human so that we might be deified is a classic statement of theosis.
10099: Maximus developed a cosmic vision of deification in which the incarnate Christ unites created and uncreated, and believers, through virtue and love, are drawn into union with God while remaining fully human.
10101: Palamas defended the hesychast monks who claimed to see the uncreated light of God in prayer, distinguishing God's essence (unparticipable) from his energies (truly participable). Councils at Constantinople in 1341 and 1351 endorsed his teaching.
10104: In a conversation recorded by his disciple Nicholas Motovilov (1831, published 1903), Seraphim taught that the true aim of the Christian life is the acquisition of the Holy Spirit, with prayer, fasting and good works as means.

10106:
Deification language appears in Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria and Athanasius, and becomes central in the Cappadocians, Maximus and the monastic tradition. The fourteenth-century hesychast controversy, in which Barlaam of Calabria challenged monks' claims to experience God's light, led Palamas to articulate the essence-energies distinction, endorsed by Byzantine councils.

The *Philokalia* (1782), an anthology of Eastern spiritual writings compiled by Nikodemos of the Holy Mountain and Makarios of Corinth, spread hesychast spirituality into Russia and later the West. Twentieth-century Orthodox theologians in exile (Lossky, Florovsky, Meyendorff) presented theosis as the heart of Orthodoxy. Since the 1970s, Western theologians have shown renewed interest in deification, including Finnish Luther research and Wesleyan dialogue with the East.
